rss_1_1792183393.title: The pianist who never played
rss_1_1792183393.text:
Her deft fingers tapped silently in the air. They had been designed to play melodies, despite never having met a piano. From the storage shed’s dusty window, she watched the newer pianist on the gorgeous grand piano in the main parlour, dreaming it was her playing instead. How could they know this other pianist played better, if they’d never even heard her perform?

The shed door creaked open and the butler walked in. His warm hands opened up the battery compartment on her back to swap out her fizzling battery. He turned to walk out, but stopped short when his eyes met her forlorn gaze.

“It’s not your fault — your arrival was delayed due to a shipping disruption, and he got so impatient, he bought a newer model at the local store … Don’t be like that. There’s still hope.” His encouragement was betrayed by a pendulous sigh.

She watched the usurper dance on the keys for what felt like eternity. Androids never got sick or tired, after all. Still, she waited. What else could she do?

When the butler returned, he carried a box. “There’s more to life than piano,” he said, revealing a knowledge module, a glowing orb of circuitry that unlocked something inside her. “Why don’t you try reading?”

Read more science fiction from Nature Futures

He unloaded an assortment of books onto the concrete floor. She cracked one open, cocking her head to glance inside. Words flowed out like musical notes, harmonizing into stories that swelled inside her. She felt characters come to life, taking bold action and seizing control of their lives. Her fingers fluttered as pages flew between them, and when the evening sun’s rays flickered away, she’d exhausted her supply of stories and resorted to reading grubby warranty manuals archived in the shed.

The butler returned regularly to replenish her books. She slowed down to an adagio pace, savouring each word as she listened to the brooding sound of Chopin floating from the house. But however captivating she found books to be, her fingers still twitched with longing for the keys of a piano.

When the entire family left on a rare outing, the butler flung open her door, haloed in the morning light. “The family is out. We’re bringing you to the piano!”

She followed breathlessly, the grassy lawn tickling her feet as she ran. She almost squealed when she emerged through the double doors of the house, greeted by a glittering chandelier and a soaring staircase. Then the radiance of the piano swept away all other thoughts.

But when they stepped into the parlour, the android pianist stood in their way with an accusatory glare. She looked to the butler. He appeared to calculate for a moment, then backpedalled. “We can’t afford to get in trouble. I’ll bring you back another day.” The piano’s delicate keys whispered and coaxed, but she shook free of their spell. She trusted the butler.

Despite failing, energy coursed within her like a supercharged battery. How close the piano had been! Now that the butler, her guiding light, had shown her what was possible, she felt like the protagonists of her books. That evening, her thoughts raced as a storm of Beethoven and Liszt rolled forth from the parlour.

As eager rays of dawn peeked into the shed, she wrapped up her review of the warranty manuals and set her plan in motion. When the owner left for work, she slipped into the house and located a floating terminal, which projected a dazzling jumble of digital programs and utilities onto the wall. Oh, how she wished she had the knowledge module for operating electronic devices instead of those awkward manuals.

She grappled with the menus until she found the android management program and filed a maintenance request. She watched from the shed as a maintenance van glided up the crescent driveway, and beamed when the butler helped the maintenance team whisk the pianist away.

Upon returning to a musicless house, the owner roared with displeasure. He interrogated the butler, “What happened to my pianist?”

“Just maintenance. I thought you —”

“I never authorized a maintenance order.”

rss_2_1792183394.title: IceCube just won a Nobel prize. Protect astroparticle physics projects with the same potential
rss_2_1792183394.text:
The IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica.Credit: Christopher Michel (CC BY-SA 4.0)

I vividly remember the first time I read one of Francis Halzen’s papers about high-energy neutrinos. It was the late 1990s, and I was an undergraduate student at the University of California, Berkeley. The field of astroparticle physics was young, and Halzen was making predictions that couldn’t be tested using conventional particle accelerators.

On 6 October, Halzen was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory at the South Pole. The experiment uses sensors embedded in the ice to detect high-energy neutrinos (a type of fundamental particle) that have been blasted towards Earth from distant cosmic accelerators.

Nobel physics prize awarded for detection of cosmic neutrinos

Astroparticle physicists have lots of ideas for experiments that have the same discovery potential as IceCube. For example, the underwater Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE) — a collaboration between North America and Europe — is currently under construction off the coast of Vancouver Island, Canada. There are also several projects searching for dark matter (a substance that does not interact with or emit light), including the XLZD Collaboration (a European–North American consortium) and PandaX in China.

However, realizing these experiments is not easy. The story of Halzen and IceCube is a lesson not just about fundamental science, but also about what it will take to build the infrastructure that will support discoveries over the next few decades.

When I first read Halzen’s paper (F. Halzen et al. Astrophys. J. 527, L93–L96; 1999), IceCube was not yet built, but its predecessor, called the Antarctic Muon and Neutrino Detector Array (AMANDA), was running. The construction of AMANDA cost around US$7 million. This is much less than the $271 million it cost to build IceCube. Nevertheless, realizing experiments at this smaller scale can be difficult. They require more resources than an initial proof-of-concept project, but they are not large enough to make a discovery.

Astronomy’s ‘adrenaline junkies’: Nobel prize captures the thrill of neutrino physics

Many countries face difficult decisions about research funding, and I am concerned that small and mid-scale projects could be an easy target for cuts. For example, the 2023 US particle physics strategic plan (P5) recommended creating a portfolio of small-scale experiments. However, because of budgetary constraints, it is unclear whether the proposed portfolio will go ahead.

rss_3_1792183395.title: Memory stays strong in old age when this brain enzyme is active
rss_3_1792183395.text:
Screening of mouse hippocampus cells (pictured) identified an enzyme whose production rose with age. Credit: Talley Lambert/Science Photo Library

An enzyme found in the brain could help to preserve cognitive resilience with advancing age, according to research in mice, humans and cells1.

Researchers found that high levels of the enzyme are linked to low levels of inflammation in the brains of aged mice. They also showed that the enzyme boosts the growth of neurons in ageing brains. The findings were reported on 15 October in Nature Neuroscience.

The enzyme seems to act “as a compensatory cognitive-resilience mechanism”, says study co-author Amar Sahay, a neuroscientist at Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston.

“This is a fantastic, very thoughtful approach to get at what could be protecting neurons,” says Timothy Hohman, a neuroscientist and geneticist at the Vanderbilt Memory & Alzheimer’s Center in Nashville, Tennessee, who was not involved in the study. “This is a great example of how you can use a model system to get at some of these resilience mechanisms that are super challenging to study in humans.”

A new neuroprotectant

The enzyme in question is a phospholipase, which breaks down fatty compounds. The authors homed in on the enzyme after finding that the gene encoding it suddenly became more active when connections between some of the neurons in the brains of mice were disrupted.

How to avoid dementia — what the science really says

To learn more, the scientists genetically altered mice to lack the gene, called Pla2g2f, and looked at what happened as they aged. The researchers saw a surge of inflammation and neuron degradation compared with the brains of unaltered control animals. By contrast, mice that had excess Pla2g2f displayed less inflammation and better-connected neurons in their brains as they got older.

The team also tested the animals’ spatial memory. These results, too, suggested that the enzyme provides protection. Middle-aged mice that were lacking Pla2g2f scored lower on the memory tests than did middle-aged control mice; older animals with boosted Pla2g2f scored higher on the test than did older control mice.

These findings show that Pla2g2f can be used to shift the trajectory of pathological ageing in mice, Sahay adds.

Human genetics

The gene might also have a protective role in humans. The authors analysed two large data sets2 compiled by other scientists and found that PLA2G2F activity in the human brain rises with age.

Sahay collaborated with researchers who had collected gene-expression data4 from the brains of deceased human donors. The donors had all undergone cognitive testing before their death. Sahay’s team found that PLA2G2F activity was highest in ‘resilient’ individuals — people whose cognition remained intact even though their brains had deposits of a protein called amyloid-β. Such deposits are a feature of Alzheimer’s disease.

rss_4_1792183397.title: Unprecedented atlas explores mitochondria across the tree of life
rss_4_1792183397.text:
The protein catalogue gives a dynamic picture of the mitochondria, beyond what was known from humans and yeast. Credit: Dr David Furness/Keele University/SPL

Scientists have mapped in unprecedented detail the proteins that make up the mitochondria in six organisms — five single-celled parasites and one plant — spanning the eukaryotic tree of life.

The findings, described in nine papers published in Cell, Cell Press Blue, Molecular Cell and Current Biology on 1 October1–9, reveal dozens of proteins that are not found in humans but are shared among parasites, including some that cause malaria or sleeping sickness. The findings might help scientists to devise new treatments for these illnesses.

The work has also stirred a long-running debate about the origin of the mitochondrion.

Cells are swapping their mitochondria. What does this mean for our health?

Best known as the powerhouse of the eukaryotic cell because it produces energy, the mitochondrion has its own tiny DNA, which is distinct from that of the cell’s nucleus. But both mitochondrial and nuclear DNA encode the proteins that make up this organelle. Most of what is known about the mitochondria comes from human and yeast studies, says Vamsi Mootha, a mitochondrial biologist at Howard Hughes Medical Institute in Boston, Massachusetts, who led the ‘mitoproteome’ catalogues project.

Now, by analysing mitochondrial proteins in several eukaryotic branches, the team has detected more proteins that might point to unstudied molecular pathways.

Trove of parasite proteins

Mootha and his colleagues analysed the proteome of several parasites, including Giardia lamblia1, which infects about 280 million people worldwide each year and causes diarrhoea10. Giardia parasites have tiny, mitochondrion-like organelles that are notoriously difficult to study because they live inside the gut of other organisms, without oxygen, says Pavel Doležal, a cell biologist at Charles University in Prague, Czech Republic.

Mootha and his colleagues identified a total of 59 mitochondrial proteins in G. lamblia — 32 that were known to scientists before and 27 new ones1. The function of 34 of these is unknown, which is surprising, Doležal says, because “it means that there is some new metabolism that we don’t know about. And it was overlooked”.

Combining the mitoproteomes from the six organisms with those known for humans and yeasts, the researchers assembled a collection of 8,619 mitochondrial proteins that charted into 3,199 families2. Around 43% of these families have not been recorded in a giant database of proteins known as Pfam. And 33 protein families are conserved in eukaryotic pathogens but absent in humans.

These proteins can be “ideal drug targets” for precise therapies that would act on parasite proteins but not human ones, Mootha says.

Obscure origins

Researchers agree that the mitochondria emerged two billion years ago when a bacterium was engulfed by an archaeal cell and began living inside it in a mutually beneficial relationship — known as endosymbiosis. This bacterium, which later became the mitochondrion, is thought to have provided its host archaea with energy.

rss_5_1792183398.title: PhD students who write dissertation with AI less likely to stay in academia
rss_5_1792183398.text:
PhD students are increasingly using AI to help write their dissertations.Credit: Ginaellen/Getty

Roughly 30% of PhD dissertations in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) in the United States this year contained AI-generated text, according to a working paper1 that reviewed the abstracts submitted to an online database since 2019.

What’s more, the working paper, which has not been peer reviewed, found that PhD graduates who use artificial intelligence to help write their dissertations are more likely to work in industry and less likely to enter academia.

Various studies have shown a marked increase in the presence of text generated using AI in scientific literature over the past few years. Researchers at the US-based non-profit organization the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) wanted to understand how PhD students use AI because insights into students’ training and capabilities will shape science over the next several decades.

“If our students are only doing half the work and they’re dishing the rest to AI, do they really have the depth of understanding” to be good scientists? asks co-author Daniel Gross, an economist at NBER who is based in Durham.

The working paper analysed dissertations from more than 226,000 STEM doctoral graduates completed between January 2019 and May 2026 at US universities. The team used the AI-detection service Pangram to assess the abstracts. For the study, the researchers categorized abstracts as either AI-written or not; they did not distinguish between text that was wholly or partly generated by AI. (Although Gross says that 90% of the flagged AI-generated abstracts were classified by Pangram as entirely AI-generated.)

The team found that AI-generated text in dissertation abstracts first appeared in 2023, and rose from 1.7% that year to 18.8% in 2025. For dissertations filed during the first five months of 2026, 29.4% of abstracts contained AI-generated text. AI use was highest in mathematical and computer sciences: 36% of the abstracts had been written using AI. About 41% of dissertations by graduates educated in non-English-speaking countries had AI-generated abstracts, compared with 23% of dissertations by those from English-speaking countries.

Ang Liu, an engineer at the University of New South Wales in Sydney, Australia, says that one issue with PhD students using generative AI tools to write their dissertations is that researchers are expected to explore areas in which the answers are not already known. AI can be extremely helpful when students are working in areas in which there is already a substantial body of knowledge, he says. However, the challenge comes when research moves into areas in which knowledge is incomplete or uncertain. “That is where rigorous research training becomes even more important,” he says.

Job pathways

The researchers also reviewed PhD graduates’ education and employment profiles on the social-media platform LinkedIn. Among PhD graduates who completed their undergraduate degrees in the United States, those with AI-generated abstracts were 17% less likely to be employed in academia than were graduates who did not use AI. However, using AI made those graduates 16% more likely to be employed in industry than those who did not use it. The authors found that the link between AI use and landing a job in academia was less pronounced for graduates who did their undergraduate studies outside the US.

rss_6_1792183399.title: History’s long-secret codes are being cracked by amateurs using AI
rss_6_1792183399.text:
Enigma machines were used by the German armed forces to encrypt communications during the Second World War.Credit: Ullstein Bild via Getty

Carter Leffen couldn’t believe his eyes when the artificial-intelligence model GPT-6 Astra decoded a secret German army message that had been encrypted for 85 years. Leffen, who has no cryptography experience, asked the model to decipher the message, nudged it a few times to keep thinking and encouraged it to keep working when he went to bed. Sure enough, when he woke up in the morning, it had a solution.

Leffen is one of many non-experts who are now using large language models (LLMs) to break historical codes. Their efforts harness the LLMs’ ability to rapidly deploy decryption algorithms while also searching the Internet for extra historical documents or information that might help.

Cryptography specialists are thrilled at the surge in interest in codebreaking — but they are also being overwhelmed by a deluge of requests to validate AI solutions, which can often be incorrect. “There are so many false positives that are coming in from people who don’t really understand cryptanalysis,” says Elonka Dunin, a retired game developer in the Washington DC area who has written books on cryptography.

Cracked codes

In September, Leffen, a product development coach at financial data and media company Bloomberg in New York City, asked GPT-6 Astra to scour Crypto Cellar Research, a website listing historical, unsolved ciphers that is run by independent cryptographer Frode Weierud in Oslo. Leffen tasked the LLM with selecting and then decoding a message encrypted by Enigma, a machine used by the German armed forces during the Second World War to hide military communications from enemies. Enigma’s rotors and plugs rerouted electrical signals to encrypt the letters of the alphabet in up to 103 sextillion possible ways.

AI is helping to decode animals’ speech. Will it also let us talk with them?

GPT-6 Astra, developed by the firm OpenAI in San Francisco, California, chose a message sent on 10 July 1941, possibly because it was short — 82 characters — and was potentially related to another Enigma message sent on the same date that had been decoded in 2017. If that already-solved message contained some of the same words as the unsolved one, it could help to ease the decryption, providing what cryptographers call a crib. For instance, both messages might be addressed to “Obergruppenführer”, a high-level Nazi official.

GPT-6 Astra wrote code to simulate an Enigma machine and searched for the settings that would both reproduce the crib from the message solved in 2017 and render the unsolved message comprehensible. In ten hours, the LLM tested more than four billion settings. Leffen was “gobsmacked” by the solution it presented to him and sent it to Weierud for confirmation. It turned out that the message had been encrypted with Enigma settings different from those used on the already-deciphered message, even though they were sent on the same day — this is unusual and might explain why the code went unsolved for so long.

The imitation game

Days later, inspired by Leffen’s success, Carter Church, a staff engineer at cybersecurity company SentinelOne in Mountain View, California, decided to tackle an unsolved cipher sent by an Italian official to one of French emperor Napoleon’s generals in 1809. Church gave GPT-6 Astra a picture of the message, which had been listed on Cryptiana, a website compiled by Japanese patent engineer and hobby cryptographer Satoshi Tomokiyo.

GPT-6 Astra found a partial key among records on a French cryptography website, and tried an incremental approach to tackle the unsolved message. It used a common decoding strategy called simulated annealing, in which a deciphering key is tweaked iteratively according to whether the output is more comprehensible than that from the previous key. GPT-6 Astra hit on a successful key in about six hours, and Church sent the decoded message — which turned out to describe troop locations — to Tomokiyo, based in Tokyo, for verification.

Carter Church used GPT-6 Astra to decode this 1809 letter, intended for a general in the French emperor Napoleon’s army.Credit: Persée/French Ministry of National Education, Higher Education and Research

Church notes that this message could have been solved without AI, but the LLM’s ability to transcribe the symbols in the image, find the partial key and determine how to apply it greatly reduced the time and effort required.

rss_8_1792183401.title: World’s timekeepers upend how they adjust time to avoid catastrophic ‘negative second’
rss_8_1792183401.text:
Metrologists retire the leap second immediately, instead of by 2035. Credit: Alejandro Martinez Velez/Europa Press via Getty

Time discrepancies that used to be adjusted by a jump of a second around once every 1.5 years will now wait until an hour needs correcting instead.

Leap seconds serve to align time given by the sun’s position in the sky, which is based on Earth’s unsteady natural rotation, with the more stable ticking of atomic clocks, known as Universal Coordinated Time (UTC). But the rogue seconds have been a thorn in timekeepers' sides, disrupting computing systems and causing misalignment between clocks on the day they are implemented.

Their replacement — a shift of an hour once Earth time and atomic time drift apart by 3,600 seconds — likely won’t be needed for thousands of years, effectively pushing the issue onto future generations.

The leap second is dead. Long live the leap hour?

Member states of the General Conference on Weights and Measures (CGPM) voted to pass the resolution at their 28th meeting, outside Paris, on 15 October.

“This decision will ensure the continuity and relevance of UTC for centuries to come,” says Georgette Macdonald, director general of the National Research Council of Canada’s Metrology Research Centre in Halifax, Canada. Canada backed the resolution, which was not supported unanimously but only needed a majority to pass, she says.

“This is a historical moment, a decisive step for UTC”, says Noël Dimarcq, a metrologist at the Côte d'Azur Observatory in Nice, France, who formally introduced the resolution. "We now have an international reference time scale [that is] continuous for the next millennia", he adds.

Computing casualties

rss_10_1792183404.title: Daily briefing: Bleached corals revived by healthy neighbour’s touch
rss_10_1792183404.text:
Ghostly white corals are fully restored in eight weeks by contact with a healthy counterpart. Plus, arXiv is capping submissions per researcher and four good news stories to brighten your day.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

In stressful conditions, corals expel the symbiotic algae that give them their colour from their tissues. Putting a bleached coral in contact with a healthy one (left) can restore it to full health within eight weeks (right).Credit: Danny Collins

Scientists have successfully restored bleached coral in the lab by placing it in contact with a healthy fragment. Researchers found that when a healthy piece of Pocillopora damicornis coral rested against a bleached piece, the two fused together to create a bridge across which algal symbionts can spread. This transfer fully restored the bleached coral within eight weeks, even if the healthy piece was removed after a week. The result “can inspire solutions that eventually may be scalable” to reverse widespread coral decline, says marine ecologist and study co-author Fiorenza Micheli.

Nature | 5 min read

Reference: Science Advances paper

The preprint server arXiv has introduced a cap of two papers per month for each submitting researcher in a bid to clampdown on a deluge of submissions, many generated by artificial intelligence. The limit is the latest measure to prevent its voluntary moderators from being overwhelmed by submissions, says astrophysicist Steinn Sigurðsson, scientific director of arXiv. Some researchers support the cap; others counter that it doesn’t solve the root problem. AI slop will “simply go somewhere else and become someone else’s problem”, says Natalie Khalil, the founder of AI-assisted peer-review platform Reviewer3.

Nature | 5 min read

A study of more than 100,000 people has revealed some surprising benefits of brown fat — a type that burns calories to generate heat. Researchers found that people with ‘active’ brown fat are less affected by health issues — such as type 2 diabetes, depression and anxiety — than those without it. The risk of these conditions decreased the more active brown fat a person had. The study is retrospective, so can’t confirm that brown fat is causing these benefits, but “it’s still a very interesting and surprising study”, says molecular biologist Irfan Lodhi.

Nature | 5 min read

Reference: Nature paper

When presented with two shapes, one with spikes and one rounded, and asked to designate them ‘bouba’ and ‘kiki’, people tend to agree that kiki is the spiky one — and so do dogs. Researchers found that when presented with images of these shapes, domestic dogs (Canis familiaris) more often looked at and moved toward the round shape when the word ‘bouba’ was played from a speaker, and vice versa. The results could suggest that dogs make similar connections between visual information and sounds to humans.

ScienceAlert | 5 min read

Reference: Proceedings of the Royal Society B paper

Features & opinion

Nature’s latest collection of stories selected to bring readers joy includes the newest penguin species described by science, and news that the island nation of Mauritius has become the first country in the world to reduce its number of people with type 2 diabetes — an impressive feat with diabetes rates rising globally, researchers say.

Nature | 5 min read

A technique called metagenomic testing can screen for every microorganism that might be present in a sample, rather than searching for one in particular. Now hospitals are trialling ways of using these tests to quickly identify whether acute illnesses that cause neurological symptoms are bacterial, viral or autoimmune in origin to inform more effective treatment. Interpreting the results of metagenomic tests — which pick up pathogens, harmless microbes and contamination alike — can be a rate-limiting step, but advances in AI have enabled a faster sort of useful data from noise.

BBC Future | 6 min read

The US National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine has updated On Being a Scientist, its bible for graduate students and early career researchers first published in 1989. Things have changed since the last edition, in 2009, note engineer Mitul Luhar, chemist and dean Emily Pentzer and psychologist Alan Leshner, who was formerly head of the American Association for the Advancement of Science. “Shifts in research priorities and funding place new expectations and pressures on scientists,” they write. “Early-career researchers feel the consequences most acutely.”

Issues in Science and Technology | 9 min read

Reference: On Being a Scientist: A Guide to the Responsible and Ethical Conduct of Research

rss_11_1792183405.title: Nearly half of reef-building corals face elevated relative risk of extinction
rss_11_1792183405.text: Coral reefs are diverse marine ecosystems that provide ecological functions and economic and social benefits across over 100 tropical countries. Warming driven by climate change is a primary threat to coral reefs and is increasing the frequency of global coral bleaching events. Here we reassessed the IUCN Red List status of 892 reef-building coral species, first assessed in 2008 1. Because species-level population trends are unavailable for most reef-building corals, population reductions were inferred using proxies based on global coral cover trends and projected annual severe bleaching under SSP2-4.5, both over three decades, adjusted using trait-based estimates of species vulnerability. Of the 774 species with sufficient data to be assessed, 340 (44%) were classified as threatened under IUCN Red List criteria. Thirty-three species were assessed as Critically Endangered, 251 as Endangered, and 56 as Vulnerable, most due to risk of population reduction associated with projected thermal stress. These findings predate the three hottest years on record and the fourth global coral bleaching event (2023-2025), and the first exceedance for an annual mean of the 1.5oC global warming threshold. The findings reinforce the importance of limiting further warming to maintain coral biodiversity and reef ecosystem function. The Red List assesses the relative extinction risk of species, whereby species are placed in categories of increasing risk by comparing their population size, decline and geographic range against standardised thresholds. The Red List does not predict whether or when a species may go extinct. As the ranges of coral species remain under-surveyed, future assessments would be strengthened by species-level population data and thermal-stress and recovery metrics that better capture range-representative dynamics.

rss_12_1792183407.title: Give me the good news: four science stories to brighten your day
rss_12_1792183407.text:
A new species of sea spider, Tanystylum kiixin, has been discovered.Credit: Cormac Toler-Scott

Amid wars, AI doom and a super El Niño, good news can seem in short supply. But it is there if you go looking. In Nature’s latest collection of stories selected to bring readers joy, learn about a country that has reversed its rates of diabetes and umbrella that keep corals cool.

But first, you might have heard about reports of the first new wild cat species in a century, announced last month1. The spotted feline, called Leopardus tilcayo, was found in the forested Yungas region of Bolivia.

The news is not all bad: five inspiring science stories to lift your mood

But did you know that a new member has also been inducted into the penguin family this year? A population of penguins on the remote Kerguelen Islands — around 2,000 kilometres north of Antarctica in the Indian Ocean — has been designated as a new species, the southeastern gentoo (Pygoscelis kerguelensis)2. This addresses a long-running debate about whether the gentoo penguin (Pygoscelis papua) is one species or several. Using genetic analysis, scientists say the southeastern gentoo is its own species and that three populations previously identified as subspecies of gentoo should also be considered their own species.

Meanwhile, two new species of sea spider3 have been found in the Salish Sea, off the west coast of the United States and Canada. Sea spiders are a type of marine arthropod related to horseshoe crabs and arachnids. One of the new species, Callipallene pilosuspedes, has four bright red eyes, legs three times as long as its body, a triangular mouth and a short proboscis with claws it uses to grab food. It also uses spiny appendages at the bottom of its head, called ovigers, to groom itself. The other species, called Tanystylum kiixin, has stubby legs, an hourglass-shaped body and black eyes.

Diabetes rates go down

Mauritius has become the first country in the world to reduce its number of people with type 2 diabetes4. Researchers say this is impressive, given that rates of the disease are rising globally.

The island nation off the east coast of Africa has been surveying how many people have type 2 diabetes or raised blood sugar levels — an indicator of being at risk of developing diabetes — since 1987. The number of people with the condition went up between 1987 and 2009, but had decreased by 11% for men and 16% for women by 2021. Rates of raised blood sugar also decreased by roughly one-third between 2009 and 2021.

The trend is striking, write Shukri Mohamed and Andre Pascal, at the African Population and Health Research Center in Nairobi, in a commentary5 accompanying the study in The Lancet Diabetes and Endocrinology. It is probably the result of improved awareness of diabetes, they say, as well as better screening and access to health care.

Umbrellas for coral

Improvised umbrellas made from cloth resistant to ultraviolet light protected a small section of coral reef in the Florida Keys from heat stress during extreme temperatures in 20246. Scientists made umbrella-like canopies using PVC pipes, filled with spray foam, and shade cloth; the structures floated about 30 centimetres above the coral.

Researchers assemble a shade covering over coral in the Florida Keys.Credit: Arelys Chaparro

This shading reduced the amount of solar radiation the coral was exposed to, minimizing the heat stress that often causes coral bleaching by killing tiny, coloured organisms that live inside the coral. Nearby unshaded corals, by comparison, continued to get paler over time. The research team says that similar shades could be a cheap, effective way to protect coral against heat stress.
